cells.tense: Right now you know what's owed and you're settling it between people as it comes.
cells.ask: Say out loud that the give and take between you two feels right — name it once where they can hear you.
cells.core:
You can feel what's owed in a room, and you act on it while it's still live. Someone shortchanges a friend, gets dismissed, gets left out, and your chest registers it before the thinking starts. That knowing isn't loud. It's your own instrument, running quietly under the conversation, and it steers what you do next.

Take the harvest that's already yours. The patient work of caring for people; the endings you let end; the effort you kept making when nothing came back — it grew something you're standing in now. Say the balance out loud when it's true. What's paying for this is that you can't keep the instrument hidden and still be easy around people. Held lightly, it's just presence.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel what's fair and act on it while it's live.
cells.verb: Weighing what's fair and what's owed
cells.place: Where two people stand close enough to feel each other

cells.tense: Somewhere ahead of you sits a reckoning you're already arguing with.
cells.ask: Let one person help you with something you'd normally carry alone, and don't audit how it went.
cells.core:
You're keeping the scales ahead of everything. Before anyone has said what they mean, you've worked out the debt, who owes what, how it should have gone. You're auditing friendships in your head at night. The instrument that tells you what's fair has started calculating instead of listening, and the planning is buying you nothing but a tighter chest.

What steadies it is borrowed strength: let one person carry something with you and don't rebalance it afterward. Someone holds the other end, resources move where they're needed, and the scales come back down to feeling. Be fair, not efficient. What this costs to keep: you stay in the room rather than refereeing it.

cells.tense: You stopped saying what you feel is owed and that door is behind you now.
cells.ask: Pick one small unfairness you let pass this week and say plainly to yourself why it stung.
cells.core:
The instrument is quiet and you've stopped trusting it. Something lands sideways and you let it sit there, telling yourself it's not worth it. The give and take around you came back crooked and you stopped keeping track. Care is still yours; you're just cautious about it, holding back the one thing that used to come naturally, which is the felt sense that something wasn't right.

The way back doesn't run through feeling yourself into closeness. It runs through small practice: a stretch of walking, a few minutes of writing something down, something you keep returning to on its own terms. Steady practice reconnects you to your own knowing faster than any forced warmth. That's the provision under this balance: not more feeling, a reliable practice.

cells.tense: You're already the one weighing what's fair between people and you call it being reasonable.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person the fairness call you've been presenting as just how things are.
cells.core:
Between you and the people around you, the fairness is coming from you — you're the one who notices the imbalance, quietly adjusts, decides what's owed. You say it's simple decency, just what any reasonable person does. It isn't automatically granted. It's your own instrument, shaping how you stand with each person you know.

Underneath that is a fullness of perception: many truths held at once, and you've had it so long you stopped noticing. Try saying the ordinary opinion out loud to one person, no support, and let it be yours. You'll likely be more right than you let on. What you see arrives without argument when you stop dressing it as common sense.

attempts.check: The draft leans on reading the person's silence and withdrawal as past harm, which the record does not support — it says only that the private sense of fairness has gone quiet, not what happened or who. A reader could reasonably say the inner weighing was never damaged, just never given a room. The ask survives a wrong read because it is an act of telling the truth bare once with no outcome demanded, useful whether the weighing is bruised or simply unpracticed. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line implying I know why the compass went quiet.
